new_statements.quote: 2.1.2. Фонологическое ударение в ГК отсутствует. Имеется два уровневых т о н а: В — высокий, Н — низкий. Есть лексический плавающий высокий тон, который всегда следует за низким и обозначается гачеком на конечном гласном слова: yàlǎ ‛лев’ [...] Контурный тон представляет собой сочетание двух фонологически уровневых. [p. 287:] Сегментная база тона в ГК — гласный. Тоны в ГК образуют фиксированные последовательности (мелодии). Сегментная база тональных последовательностей — с т о п а (см. 2.2.1.). Непроизводные морфемы группируются в 6 тональных классов, из которых 6-й является наименее частотным.
new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. Phonological stress is absent in GK [Guinean Kpelle]. There are two level tones: H (high) and L (low). There is a lexical floating high tone, which always follows a low tone and is marked with a háček on the final vowel of the word: yàlǎ 'lion' [...] A contour tone is a combination of two phonologically level tones. [p. 287:] The segmental base of tone in GK is the vowel. Tones in GK form fixed sequences (melodies). The segmental base of tonal sequences is the foot (see 2.2.1). Non-derived morphemes are grouped into 6 tonal classes, of which the 6th is the least frequent.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (classification tonal-OR-pitch accent from Konoshenko 2019/2008 and Konoshenko & Uvarova 2025) notes those sources are silent on stress ('No word-stress rule stated anywhere'). This chapter is compatible (same binary H/L system, floating H, the same six melodies) and adds the explicit statement that phonological stress is absent, which upgrades 'silent on stress' to an explicit no-word-stress claim and names the melody domain (the foot).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The source states outright that Guinean Kpelle has no phonological stress. Word prosody is tonal: two level tones H and L plus a lexical floating H (always after L, written on the word-final vowel), organized into six fixed lexical melodies /H/, /L(H)/, /HL/, /LHL/, /L/, /LH/ whose domain is the 'foot' (стопа, §2.2.1, p. 290), a cohesion unit defined by vowel co-occurrence restrictions, nasal harmony, consonant distribution and fixed tone melodies, not by any prominence peak. Grammatical replacive melodies /L/ and /L(H)/ also exist (pp. 287-288).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable; nothing on secondary stress or any prominence (no stress at all per the source).
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Tonal notes: the Tongonaaloi subdialect has a marginal mid tone (contextual on verbs, lexical in a few function words and in CVCVCV(V) nouns; p. 286-287); /LH/ melody is marginal and cannot surface on CVV in the Honkwele subdialect described (p. 291, §2.2.1); /L(H)/ vs /L/ neutralize before a high tone (p. 287, note 3).
new_statements.identity_note: Konoshenko 2017 states (p. 285, §2.0.0) that it describes central Guinean Kpelle, specifically the Honkwele (хонквеле) subdialect spoken in Nzérékoré, with material from the Tongonaaloi (тонгонаалой) subdialect and the northern Gbali (гбали) dialect flagged where used; the no-stress statement is made for 'ГК' (Guinean Kpelle) generally. Konoshenko & Khachaturyan 2024 concerns Guinean Kpelle (Guerzé, iso gkp) of Forest Guinea as the contact language of Mano; its main object is Mano final lowering, with Kpelle L1 speakers as a baseline. Neither work covers Liberian Kpelle (libe1247).

tone_statements.quote: Guinean Kpelle is a tone language featuring a binary L vs. H contrast. The tonal elements make up fixed melodies, e.g., the most common are /H/, /Lᴴ/, /HL/, /LHL/, /L/, and /LH/ is marginal, as shown in Table 1. ... Items having /Lᴴ/ melody end with a phonological floating ᴴ; orthographically they are represented with a caron on the first vowel: yǎla ‘lion’, pǎa ‘kill’. ... There are replacive grammatical tones, e.g., {L} marking the verb in some TAM constructions; on a par with additive tonal prefixes
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones in fixed word melodies /H/, /Lᴴ/ (final floating H, superscript in print), /HL/, /LHL/, /L/, marginal /LH/; H/L tonal prefixes; downstepped H; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Green, Christopher R. & Maria Konoshenko. 2022. Tonal head marking in Mande compounds: endpoint neutralization and outliers. Mandenkan 67: 3-44. doi:10.4000/mandenkan.2699
tone_statements.quote: GK features a binary /H/ vs. /L/ contrast. There is no evidence that either tone is unmarked since they are both morphophonologically active in the language, with H and L tone prefixes marking a particular syntactic type of 1SG and 3SG pronominals, respectively. The majority of lexemes in GK are associated with a limited number of basic tonal melodies: /H/, /Lᴴ/, /HL/, /LHL/, /LH/, /L/. The /HL/ melody always surfaces as [H.HL] on bisyllabic structures. Verbs and inherently possessed nouns do not have lexical /L/.
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H vs L; lexemes carry melodies H, L+floating H, HL, LHL, LH, L; grammatical lowering to {L}, High Spread, Contour Simplification; ~70+ tone-marked forms; nothing on stress or TBU.

tone_statements.quote: In Guinean Kpelle, verbs have underlying lexical tone melodies /H/, /LH/, /HL/ and /LHL/; the lexical melodies appear in various TAMP constructions. There is no lexical /L/ on verbs, but this melody appears as a grammatical replacive {L} tone. ... In Guinean Kpelle, grammatical {L} marker is phonologically transparent after Low tone ... However, if the preceding syntactic element ends with High tone, the {L} on the verb undergoes High spread (7). ... If the following word bears initial High, it gets downstepped
tone_statements.summary: Verb melodies /H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/ built from H and L; replacive grammatical {L} and {LH}; H spread gives surface [HL] falling; downstep. No tone-level count given for Kpelle; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Konoshenko, Maria. 2020. Good nouns, naughty verbs: How French borrowings receive grammatical tones in Guinean Kpelle. Language in Africa 1(4): 131-145. doi:10.37892/2686-8946-2020-1-4-131-145
tone_statements.quote: GK is a two-tone language with contrastive H and L. These tones combine to produce six main word level tone patterns, which may be lexical or contextual: [Table 1: /H/ High throughout; /HL/ High falling; /LHL/ Low falling; /L(H)/ Low flat; /L/ Low falling; /LH/ Low high] In certain constructions, grammatical replacive {L} tone completely rewrites lexical tones of nouns and verbs.

tone_statements.quote: 6.1. В отличие от либерийского кпелле, в центральном гвинейском кпелле противопоставляются только два «полноценных» тональных уровня: высокий и низкий. Что касается среднего тона, то в одних случаях он является контекстно обусловленным -см. далее п. 6.4.3., в других случаях он оказывается частью тоне-мы некоторых трехсложных слов, которых очень мало (около 10). [...] 7.1. В гбали противопоставляются только два уровневых тона: высокий и низкий. Среднего тона - ни контекстно обусловленного, ни закрепленного лексически - в этом диалекте нет.
tone_statements.translation: 6.1. Unlike Liberian Kpelle, central Guinean Kpelle opposes only two 'full' tone levels: high and low. As for the mid tone, in some cases it is contextually conditioned (see 6.4.3 below), in other cases it turns out to be part of the toneme of certain trisyllabic words, which are very few (about 10). [...] 7.1. In Gbali only two level tones are opposed: high and low. There is no mid tone in this dialect, neither contextually conditioned nor lexically fixed.

tone_statements.citation: Konoshenko, Maria. 2008. Tonal systems in three dialects of the Kpelle language. Mandenkan 44: 21-42.
tone_statements.quote: the core difference between the nominal tonal classes in Guinean and Liberian Kpelle is that the latter uses mid tone as a basic suprasegmental unit, while the former does not. ... In Gbali the mid tone (phonetically, a mid level of pitch) is extremely marginal and morphophonologically conditioned ..., in other words, there are only 2 basic levels of pitch relevant for this dialect. In SGK the mid tone is more relevant, ... and “latent” mid tonal pattern can even be considered as lexically assigned to class 2 verbs.
tone_statements.locator: p. 27 (end of section 2, before table 9) and p. 39, section 4 'Summary', 'number of pitch level oppositions'
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H/L, one per syllable, in 5 lexical tonal classes; falling HL = H+L on one syllable; mid marginal (Gbali) or latent (SGK), basic only in Liberian; floating H and L; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.summary: A syncretic replacive Low marks the Preterite and Habitual (both polarities), Prohibitive, Conjoint and Conditional, and its surface form is obscured by High spread ([HL] after a High object, simplified to [H] with downstep on a following High); a {LH} replacive with suffix -nì marks the Stative participle. There is no lexical /L/ on verbs, but this melody appears as a grammatical replacive {L} tone. ... In Guinean Kpelle, grammatical {L} marker is phonologically transparent after Low tone ... However, if the preceding syntactic element ends with High tone, the {L} on the verb undergoes High spread (7). ... If the following word bears initial High, it gets downstepped

sources.quote: GK is a two-tone language with contrastive H and L. These tones combine to produce six main word level tone patterns, which may be lexical or contextual: [Table 1: /H/ High throughout; /HL/ High falling; /LHL/ Low falling; /L(H)/ Low flat; /L/ Low falling; /LH/ Low high] In certain constructions, grammatical replacive {L} tone completely rewrites lexical tones of nouns and verbs.

sources.note: Loanword tonology: GK is a two-tone language (H vs L) whose tones combine into six word-level patterns /H/, /HL/, /LHL/, /L(H)/, /L/, /LH/; describes grammatical replacive {L} tone on compound heads, possessed nouns and verbs in certain TAM constructions, prefixal grammatical tones, consonant alternation with tone, surface tone rules and downstep; French loan nouns follow native lexical and grammatical tone rules fully, loan verbs only partly ('naughty verbs').

tone.translation: 6.1. Unlike Liberian Kpelle, central Guinean Kpelle opposes only two 'full' tone levels: high and low. As for the mid tone, in some cases it is contextually conditioned (see 6.4.3 below), in other cases it turns out to be part of the toneme of certain trisyllabic words, which are very few (about 10). [...] 7.1. In Gbali only two level tones are opposed: high and low. There is no mid tone in this dialect, neither contextually conditioned nor lexically fixed.

sources.quote: the core difference between the nominal tonal classes in Guinean and Liberian Kpelle is that the latter uses mid tone as a basic suprasegmental unit, while the former does not. ... In Gbali the mid tone (phonetically, a mid level of pitch) is extremely marginal and morphophonologically conditioned ..., in other words, there are only 2 basic levels of pitch relevant for this dialect. In SGK the mid tone is more relevant, ... and “latent” mid tonal pattern can even be considered as lexically assigned to class 2 verbs.

sources.note: Two level tones H/L, one per syllable, in 5 lexical tonal classes; falling HL = H+L on one syllable; mid marginal (Gbali) or latent (SGK), basic only in Liberian; floating H and L; nothing on stress.

tone.quote: My strongest case involves Guinean Kpelle (Southwestern Mande), as described in (Konoshenko 2014), and also based on my unpublished field data. ... In Guinean Kpelle, there is a general morphophonological rule of H spreading onto a rightward adjacent L which equally applies to different low‑level syntactic phrases ... just like Central Mande, Soso‑Southwestern Mande have binary tonal systems with a tendency towards spreading phenomena ... the tonal contrast in Soso‑Southwestern Mande is not privative in that both H and L are phonologically active.
